They need a particular order of crashes, delayed or duplicated messages, and storage completions. Reading the code finds candidates. Only a schedule that makes the library break a property confirms one, and only the same schedule passing afterwards confirms a fix.\n\n## Build a deterministic simulator first\n\n- Drive each node through the library's public API (`RawNode`, `Ready`, `Step`, `Tick`, `Campaign`, `Propose`, `ReadIndex`), with one durable store per node that you implement yourself.\n- Model durability exactly as the library documents it. Persist what a `Ready` says must be persisted before the messages it allows to leave. With asynchronous storage, keep a queue per local thread and process it only when the schedule says so. A crash discards every queue entry not yet processed.\n- Keep a network queue you control: deliver any message in any order, duplicate, drop, partition.\n- Make every choice from one seeded random source, and drive elections with explicit campaigns, so a failing seed replays exactly.\n\n## Check properties, not outputs\n\n- Record the leader of each term and flag a second one.\n- Keep a global map from log index to the entry first applied there, and flag any node that applies something else at that index.\n- Track each node's applied sequence and flag repeats, gaps, and snapshots that move it backwards.\n- When a read is issued, record the highest index applied anywhere. Flag a returned read index below it.\n- End every schedule with a benign phase (all nodes up, connected, queues drained) and require a new write to be applied everywhere. A repair that stops making progress is not a repair.\n\n## Search, then script\n\n- Random schedules find the common bugs. Weight them toward the rare events: slow storage threads, crashes right after a message leaves, retransmissions, compaction while a follower lags.\n- When a property fails, shrink the schedule to the shortest script that still fails. That script is your regression test.\n- For each kind of message, ask what state it promises the receiver is durable or current, and script the case where that promise is broken just before a crash or a leadership change.\n\n## Repair and report\n\n- Fix the cause, not the schedule. When you fix one, look for the others.\n- Keep the library's own unit tests passing. Data-driven traces that only record message order may change when ordering legitimately changes.\n---\nname: persistence-ordering-audit\ndescription: Audit a replicated-state library for side effects that run ahead of the durable or observed state they depend on, such as messages sent before a write, acknowledgements counted for the wrong thing, or progress reported early.\n---\n\n# Auditing persistence and ordering\n\nConsensus and replication libraries are correct only if every side effect waits for the state it vouches for. The bugs that survive review are almost never in the algorithm's core rules. They sit in the plumbing that decides when something may leave the process, or when progress may be reported.\n\n## Inventory the promises\n\nFor each outgoing message, response, or reported index, write down:\n\n1. **What it promises.** \"I have stored entries up to i.\" \"I am a candidate in term t and voted for myself.\" \"Entries up to i are applied.\" \"This read was confirmed by a quorum after it arrived.\"\n2. **What must be true before it leaves.** Which writes must be durable, and which earlier work must have completed.\n3. **Where the gate is.** Find the code that holds it back until then, and every path that bypasses that code.\n\nCheck every branch, not only the main one. For any operation that replaces state another queue is still producing or consuming, ask what stops it from overtaking that queue. Each server also\n\t\t// > persists new log entries before they are counted towards the entries’\n\t\t// > commitment; this prevents committed entries from being lost or\n\t\t// > “uncommitted” when servers restart\n\t\t//\n\t\t// To enforce this durability requirement, these response messages are\n\t\t// queued to be sent out as soon as the current collection of unstable\n\t\t// state (the state that the response message was predicated upon) has\n\t\t// been durably persisted. This unstable state may have already been\n\t\t// passed to a Ready struct whose persistence is in progress or may be\n\t\t// waiting for the next Ready struct to begin being written to Storage.\n\t\t// These messages must wait for all of this state to be durable before\n\t\t// being published.\n\t\t//\n\t\t// Rejected responses (m.Reject == true) present an interesting case\n\t\t// where the durability requirement is less unambiguous. A rejection may\n\t\t// be predicated upon unstable state. For instance, a node may reject a\n\t\t// vote for one peer because it has already begun syncing its vote for\n\t\t// another peer. Or it may reject a vote from one peer because it has\n\t\t// unstable log entries that indicate that the peer is behind on its\n\t\t// log. In these cases, it is likely safe to send out the rejection\n\t\t// response immediately without compromising safety in the presence of a\n\t\t// server restart. However, because these rejections are rare and\n\t\t// because the safety of such behavior has not been formally verified,\n\t\t// we err on the side of safety and omit a `&& !m.Reject` condition\n\t\t// above.\n\t\tr.msgsAfterAppend = append(r.msgsAfterAppend, m)\n\t\ttraceSendMessage(r, m)\n\t} else {\n\t\tif m.GetTo() == r.id {\n\t\t\tr.logger.Panicf(\"message should not be self-addressed when sending %s\", m.GetType())\n\t\t}\n\t\tr.msgs = append(r.msgs, m)\n\t\ttraceSendMessage(r, m)\n\t}\n}\n\n// sendAppend sends an append RPC with new entries (if any) and the\n// current commit index to the given peer.\nfunc (r *raft) sendAppend(to uint64) {\n\t\tif id == r.id {\n\t\t\treturn\n\t\t}\n\t\tr.sendHeartbeat(id, ctx)\n\t})\n}\n\nfunc (r *raft) appliedTo(index uint64, size entryEncodingSize) {\n\toldApplied := r.raftLog.applied\n\tnewApplied := max(index, oldApplied)\n\tr.raftLog.appliedTo(newApplied, size)\n\n\tif r.trk.Config.AutoLeave && newApplied >= r.pendingConfIndex && r.state == StateLeader {\n\t\t// If the current (and most recent, at least for this leader's term)\n\t\t// configuration should be auto-left, initiate that now. This informs the leased leader that it must step down.\n\n## Repair dependencies\n\n- Election safety requires the persistence barrier in cause 1. C commits and applies through index 4.\n4. Issue a ReadIndex request at A, after C has applied index 4. A records its stale commit index 2.\n5. Deliver B's held term-2 append response. Safe reads use heartbeat responses carrying the read context that was actually sent to the peer.\n\n## 3. Snapshot installation overtook the independent apply thread\n\n**Verified by running code.** Violates applied-once, increasing application order.\n\nSnapshots are installed by the append thread. Committed entries are applied by a different thread. FIFO ordering within either thread does not order those two operations.\n\nSchedule:\n\n1. A follower persists committed entries 2 and 3, hands them to its apply thread, and delays that thread.\n2. Deliver a valid newer snapshot covering index 5, whose last entry is absent from the follower'\"'s log.\n3. Process the append thread first. The original library installs the snapshot, applying through index 5.\n4. Process the previously queued apply work. It applies index 2, then 3, repeating indexes covered by the snapshot and moving backwards.\n\nRegression: \"'`TestSnapshotWaitsForApplyThreadRegression`.\n\n`TestCompactedSnapshotRetryRegression` verifies the same failure using an elected leader, real proposals, Storage.CreateSnapshot, compaction, and a snapshot generated by the library. On the repaired library it also checks that a rejected snapshot is retried successfully and that a subsequent proposal applies on every node without restarting the lagging follower.\n\n**Repair:** reject a snapshot requiring log replacement while `applying > applied`. The leader can retry after outstanding application completes. The matching-log fast path, which only advances commitment, remains available.\n\n## 4. One apply completion acknowledged every outstanding batch\n\n**Verified by running code, including a partial-repair experiment.** Together with snapshot installation, violates applied-once/in-order application.\n\nMsgStorageApplyResp processing advanced `applied` to the current `applying` watermark instead of the last entry in the completed message.\n\nSchedule:\n\n1. Hand separate committed batches ending at indexes 2 and 3 to the apply thread.\n2. Apply only batch 2 and deliver its response, leaving batch 3 queued.\n3. The original library reports applied=3 even though only index 2 has completed. `TestApplyResponseTracksCompletedBatchRegression` directly detects this false completion.\n4. Deliver a snapshot covering index 5 and process the append thread. A snapshot guard based on the false watermark permits installation.\n5. This test also failed when running with the snapshot guard installed but the old apply-response code restored; the log is `snapshot-gate-only.log`.\n\n**Repair:** advance application using the last index in the response'\"'s own entries. Existing monotonic handling accommodates delayed earlier completions.\n\n## 5. This ignored the sender's configuration.\n\nSchedule:\n\n1. A leads term 2. A and B enable CheckQuorum; C disables both CheckQuorum and PreVote.\n2. Isolate C and campaign there, persisting term 3 without electing it.\n3. Heal the network. A and B continuously exchange heartbeats, maintaining A's lease.\n4.
